articles.title: Inflation och riksbanksprotokoll
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Världens börser återhämtade sig tydligt igår efter förra veckans nedgångar. Nasdaq steg med 2,7 procent, återigen med teknikbolagen som draglok – trots börsfall för Nvidia, vars 
VD, Jensen Huang, utreds av FBI
. Det glada humöret har fortsatt i Asien under morgonen, med Nikkei upp 3 procent och Kospi över 4 procent. Oljepriset föll ytterligare under gårdagen och fortsätter ned under morgonen efter att Trump sagt att kriget med Iran är ”effectively over” militärt sett. Dollarn försvagades på bred front och svenska kronan stärktes mot de flesta valutor. Börsterminer tyder på positiv öppning i Europa och USA.
Idag väntas bland annat norsk och dansk inflation, svensk produktionsdata, riksbanksprotokoll och en rad tal från ECB, BOE och Fed, och i eftermiddag riktas ögonen mot amerikansk KPI. Idag inleds också förhandlingar om kriget i Ukraina i Abu Dhabi.
Ny Nordic Outlook ute!
Tillväxten utmanas av stigande räntor och höga energipriser, men trots allt växer global BNP med drygt 3 procent i år. 
Efter två veckors publicering av enskilda ekonomier är det idag dags att knyta ihop säcken och vi publicerar vår internationella överblick 
här
. 
Den amerikanska
 kärninflationen steg troligen med 0,25 procent i oktober
 jämfört med föregående månad, vilket är något högre än trenden tidigare i år. Det finns vissa tecken på indirekta effekter av höga energipriser, och allt tydligare indikationer på stigande pristryck på IT- och elektronikvaror. Även hyrorna tycks ha börjat stiga i snabbare takt efter att ha trendat nedåt de senaste fyra åren. Totalinflationen steg troligen också i oktober, men den senaste tidens prisnedgångar på råolja och bensin tyder på att inflationen kommer att avta framöver. På grund av nedstängningen av statsapparaten förra året publiceras inga årstakter i dag.
Vi tror att norsk kärninflation (KPI-JAE) sjönk två tiondelar till 2,8 procent i oktober
, vilket är en tiondel lägre än Norges Banks prognos. Inflationsutsikterna är blandade. Matinflationen saktade in ordentligt under sommaren men var oväntat hög i september, trots ett dämpat pristryck i grannländerna. Varuprisökningarna saktar sannolikt in under 2027, inte minst med hjälp av den kraftiga förstärkningen av NOK i år. Höga lönekostnader innebär dock troligen att tjänsteprisinflationen fortsätter att vara förhöjd under hela nästa år.
Sverige
Idag skulle Ulf Kristersson (M) ha rapporterat om eventuella framsteg i regeringsfrågan
, men sonderingsuppdraget förlängs till 
slutet av veckan
 på grund av den islossning som uppstått efter att Sverigedemokraterna släppt kraven på ministerpostrar.
Starkt momentum i svenskt näringsliv väntas ha avtagit i september.
 Efter fem månader med stigande produktion i näringslivet tror vi på en mindre sättning i slutet av kvartalet. Uppväxlingen hittills i år är bredbaserad men särskilt tydlig inom industrin, och indikatorer tyder på fortsatt optimism framöver. I en 
ny konjunkturrapport
 spår Teknikföretagen en stark tillväxt i industrisektorn både i år och nästa år, rapporterar Ekot. De är också optimistiska kring behovet av att anställa fler i sektorn nästa år.
Spännande riksbanksprotokoll.
 Samtliga direktionsledamöter ställde sig bakom beslutet att höja räntan förra veckan. I pressmeddelandet konstaterades att det är ”sannolikt att styrräntan höjs ytterligare det närmaste året, i linje med styrränteprognosen i september” – en vag formulering som öppnar för att gå försiktigt fram. Riksbankschef Erik Thedéen lät dock mer hökaktig på presskonferensen än vad som framgick av själva pressmeddelandet, vilket också har varit fallet tidigare. Vi tror att protokollet fortsätter att visa på divergerande uppfattningar bland ledamöterna när det gäller tidpunkten för nästa höjning. Göran Hjelm indikerar troligen att nedsideriskerna kring räntebanan har ökat, medan Anna Seim sannolikt argumenterar för fler höjningar.

articles.title: Growth challenged by rising interest rates and high energy prices
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext: Despite global uncertainty, energy market imbalances and rising interest rates, global GDP is growing by just over 3 per cent a year. We marginally raise our growth forecast. Investment in areas including AI, defence and energy, an improving manufacturing cycle and stable labour markets provide support. At the same time, already downbeat households face rising borrowing costs, higher inflation and growing stock market uncertainty, challenging the drivers of growth and casting doubt on the strength of the expansion. So far, the rise in inflation has mainly been driven by high energy prices. The longer energy market imbalances persist, the greater the risk of spillovers to other parts of the economy. Inflation concerns will prompt the ECB and the Fed to raise rates once or twice more before cutting towards the end of the forecast period. We raise our Swedish GDP forecast for this year but see increasing headwinds from energy prices and interest rates next year. The Riksbank will raise its policy rate once more, to 2.25 per cent in March 2027, and keep it at that level throughout 2028.

articles.title: Tillväxten utmanas av stigande räntor och höga energipriser
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Swe)
articles.fulltext: Trots global osäkerhet, obalanser på energimarknaden och stigande räntor växer global BNP med drygt 3 procent per år. Vi reviderar upp tillväxtprognosen marginellt. Investeringar inom bland annat AI, försvar och energi, en industrikonjunktur som växlar upp samt stabila arbetsmarknader ger stöd. Samtidigt möter redan deppiga hushåll stigande lånekostnader, högre inflation och en tilltagande börsoro, vilket utmanar tillväxtkrafterna och skapar osäkerhet kring konjunkturstyrkan. Inflationsuppgången drivs hittills främst av höga energipriser, men ju längre obalanserna på energimarknaden kvarstår, desto större är risken för spridningseffekter till andra delar av ekonomin. Inflationsoro får ECB och Fed att höja räntan ytterligare en eller två gånger, innan de sänker mot slutet av prognosperioden. Vi höjer BNP-prognosen för i år för Sverige men ser ökade motvindar från energi och räntor nästa år. Riksbankens styrränta höjs ytterligare en gång till 2,25 procent i mars 2027 och ligger kvar på den nivån under 2028.

articles.title: Excess liquidity squeeze and SEK buying
articles.heading: Sweden 360
articles.fulltext:
Sweden 360 provides you with a quick and broad overview of Swedish macro, rates and FX.
*** See attachment for full report ***
Macro highlights: Nordic Outlook Update – Sweden macro projections
Stronger near-term growth: 
We lift 2026 GDP growth to 3.0% (from 2.7%), reflecting stronger momentum and likely upward revisions to Q3.
Households face a tougher backdrop: 
Higher energy prices, mortgage rates and fading fiscal support are expected to slow consumption growth, and we have cut the 2027 GDP forecast to 2.5% (from 2.9%).
Industry remains the brightest spot: 
Swedish manufacturing continues to outperform peers, with exports and investment, particularly in 
defence
, telecom, pharmaceuticals and electrical equipment, expected to be the main growth drivers in 2027.
Inflation bump is temporary: 
Energy and tax effects should lift headline inflation towards 3% in early 2027, but underlying inflation remains contained and is expected to move back towards target during 2028.
New Riksbank call: 
Following softer inflation and more dovish communication, we shift the next hike to March and expect the policy rate to peak at 2.25%, remaining unchanged through end-2028 (more below).
Nordic Outlook Update: 
SEB Research
Rates highlights (I): 
Riksbank - A final rate hike in March
New call: 
The forecast is revised from two additional hikes in 2027 (February and May) to one final 25bp hike in March, with the policy rate peaking at 2.25%. 
October CPIF ex-energy came in well below expectations, marking the third consecutive downside surprise and fully reversing the high prints over the summer.
Riksbank guidance signals less urgency. 
While formally maintaining the September rate path, we interpret the Riksbank's statement that it is "likely that the policy rate will be raised further in the coming year” as deliberately vague and softer than previous communication. The dovish g
lobal repricing also reduces the pressure on the Riksbank to tighten further. 
Stronger growth
 implies that there are upside risks to our rate forecast, and 
Minutes (Tue) 
are likely to reveal diverging views on the timing for the next rate hike.
Rates highlights (II): 
Riksbank funding of FX reserve, money market liquidity and Stibor-OIS
Riksbank to fund 200bn of FX reserve with debt (I)
Starting 2027, t
he Riksbank plans to reduce FX risks in the FX reserve by borrowing foreign currency via the NDO equivalent to ~SEK 200bn. The Riksbank will a) buy SEK and b) replace existing FX swaps, each amounting to around SEK100bn. 
The measure is expected to take 12-18 months and will 
reduce the banking system’s liquidity surplus by 200bn.
This will tighten short-end krona liquidity significantly and is likely to cause further volatility. While year-end effects currently keep Stibor low, 
f
orwards
 indicate a spread of ~30bps. We 
expect higher volatility and see 
upside risks to the spread, keeping the whole front-end term structure high
. SEK56bn matures off the Riksbank’s balance sheet this week, offering a first test. 
Structural upward pressure in 
fwds
 is also likely spill over to 
xxcy
 markets, while the Riksbank’s unwinding of current FX swaps reduces 3m/6m pressure.
Further information will be provided in December, along with a formal decision. Given recent bouts of spiking overnight spreads, the 
pressure increases on the Riksbank to complement this measure with others to alleviate stress in the banking system. 
One such could be lowering the standing deposit facility rate, thereby forcing inactive participants in the banking system to manage liquidity more actively. 
Riksbank to fund 200bn of FX reserve with debt (II)
This measure means that the Debt Office will issue the equivalent of SEK200bn in FX debt for re-lending to the Riksbank. 
The Riksbank has previously funded parts of the FX reserve but decided to self-finance the reserve in 2021. During 2016-2021, the NDO only borrowed in FX bonds on behalf of the Riksbank. After the Riksbank’s decision to repay loans, supply has been kept to a minimum to maintain market presence. 
A SEK200bn increase in FX debt over 12-18 months will be a massive shift, which could 
on the margin 
reduce the downward risk on SGB supply
 given strong government finances, 
as
planned FX bond issuance may be re-directed to SGBs.
More FX bonds reduce the prospect of foreigners returning to SGBs, which should be 
marginally negative for SGB demand
. At the same time, the measure reduces Riksbank certificates and 
demand for shorter SGBs/T-bills for regulatory purposes should increase
. 
Overall, this measure also increases government debt by the same amount, bringing Maastricht debt-to-GDP above the debt anchor. This is, however, unlikely to have any notable implications for neither SGB issuance nor the fiscal outlook.
Rates highlights (III): Closing trade views
Swedish rates have had a substantial correction after a ’soft hike’ by the Riksbank and the big downside surprise in inflation. 
A big part of the 
inflation surprises over the past 6 months have come from the ‘package holidays’ component and was the likely cause of a downside surprise at the last reading as well. 
Bigger picture this inflation component should be rising into 2027 on the back of jet-fuel prices.
As such the this is a decent opportunity to 
take profit on received positions in the front-end (March 27 FRA)
.
In addition, we chose to 
close receive 1Y1Y Stibor vs ESTR
, as there too much uncertainty on the path for France & ECB rates.
FX highlights (I): SEK benefits 
on short covering & French stress; positive regime potential in 2027
FX highlights (II): 
The Riksbank is buying krona again, but support looks marginal
The Riksbank’s 2023 hedge left a clear but temporary footprint in SEK. 
During the four months of sales, the residuals in our factor model were mostly negative, and EURSEK fell from about 11.9 to 11.0 by mid-December. The effect did not last. Residuals turned positive as soon as the sales ended in late January, and EURSEK was back near 11.7 by April. 
The same method picks up the earlier flow-driven episodes in NOKSEK, which suggests it is capturing flows rather than noise. 
The Riksbank’s new plans to fund the FX reserve by FX loans via the NDO will lead to around SEK 100bn of net krona buying.
 That is a similar amount to the roughly SEK 110bn in 2023 but spread over a period three to four times as long and announced well in advance. 
The 2023 episode
 points to marginal and mostly temporary support for SEK.
No formal decision has been taken, but 
the 
Riksbank 
is highly likely to go through with this measure. A formal decision and more details on the implementation will be presented 
a
t
the December meeting.
Upcoming data and events: What to watch
Private sector production (Tue) 
is expected to decline slightly in September after being strong the last 4-5 months. 
Household consumption (Thu) 
in October is also expected to decline, partly for the same reason. 
Both production and consumption imply
 that that
final Q3 GDP (presented November 27) will be revised higher compared to the flash estimate (0.4%, 2.8% y/y). 
Final CPI (Thu): 
Flash CPIF ex energy was 0.3pp below our forecast and 0.5pp below the Riksbank’s estimate. Declining prices on package holidays is probably important for the downside surprise, but other prices were also lower. The underlying trend for package holidays is likely to be upwards, but we predict prices will fall further in November.
Riksbank minutes (Tue)
 will give important information on the different Board members’ considerations for monetary policy. Was there broad support for the slightly dovish assessment that “it is likely that the policy rate will be raised further in the coming year”?
Week Ahead:

articles.title: AI is not black and white – reflections on a dramatic week
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
Financial markets struggling to draw conclusions – some reflections.
 A highly 
expected
 shift in control of both chambers of the US Congress – but with an 
unexpectedly
 decisive political outcome
 – triggered dramatic market moves as everyone struggles to draw short- and long-term conclusions about the implications for the economy, technology and geopolitics. 
Wednesday’s positive stock market reaction surprised yours truly just as much as Thursday’s sharp sell-off.
 We already knew before the midterms that the AI and tech sectors would face increasing headwinds in the US – and elsewhere. The fact that 
Trump and the Republicans will now need to pursue domestic, foreign, security and trade policies over the next two years
 that deliver lower (energy) prices and interest rates for voters and businesses, while turning the words "America First" into reality, could eventually have a calming effect on markets. But anyone expecting Trump to become more predictable, let alone more cooperative, risks being disappointed. 
The appointment of Miller as his new chief of staff reinforces this view.
A hesitant rebound – some conclusions.
 US equities rebounded on Friday after Thursday’s sharp declines. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed 0.3% and 1.1% higher, respectively. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was still down 3.4% over the week, wiping out roughly a third of this year's gains. Analysts – and economists – now need to distinguish between current AI valuations and the long-term implications of transformative technologies for growth, inflation and productivity. The US economy's solid growth prospects were also confirmed on Friday by 
another show of strength from the US labour market
. Markets now price in a 76% probability that the Fed will raise its policy rate to 4.25% on 9 December. Brent crude is trading at USD 98 per barrel early on Monday, down 16% over the past week. 
Nvidia’s statements regarding both the 
investigation into leaked information
 and 
Jensen’s affair
 are contributing to some nervousness surrounding the company. Asian markets are following through on the gains after Friday’s rebound on Wall Street. Equity futures are trading cautiously, but with a positive bias.
Not black and white – AI's potential remains extremely difficult to assess.
 Today, there is a temptation to view AI technology as either a saviour or a threat, as heaven or hell. The truth lies somewhere in between. The question is simply where. 
Recommended reading
 (in Swedish): 
A column in Affärsvärlden – 
"AI is redrawing the map for central banks"
.
Putin wants peace talks – but does he want peace?
 Tomorrow, trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US will begin at official level in Abu Dhabi. The meeting is expected to last two days and will focus on security guarantees and steps to de-escalate the war, among other issues. 
The Kremlin's continued aggressive actions, however, show little sign of a genuine willingness to make peace
. But the shift in the balance of power in the US Congress (although it will not take effect until 3 January 2027) could introduce new tactical elements into the peace process. But it bears repeating: 
Trump's unpredictability is set in stone.
A change of prime minister?
 Israeli President 
Herzog has tasked Netanyahu challenger Gadi Eisenkot
 (leader of the newly formed Yashar Party) with forming a coalition commanding a majority in the Knesset within 28 days, with a possible extension. These political negotiations are also taking place in a new US political context. The situation in the Middle East remains serious, and the risk of further large-scale 
US military strikes
 persists following the US elections. 
Worth noting:
Qatar is seeking an agreement that would give UN nuclear inspectors access to Iran's nuclear facilities
.
Climate – COP31 kicks off today.
 Follow the latest news and developments 
here
.
Nordic key stories
Is Sweden alone in the universe?
 Tomorrow’s Riksbank minutes – from the 3 November meeting, when the Executive Board unanimously decided to raise the policy rate to 2.00% – already seem somewhat outdated in light of 
October’s surprisingly low inflation
. But monetary policy is, of course, forward-looking. There are signs – e.g. companies’ pricing plans and anecdotal evidence – that price pressures will increase ahead, but hardly dramatically. With other central banks, such as the Fed, ECB and Norges Bank, operating with significantly higher policy rates and in some cases expected to hike again, the question is relevant: 
are we alone in the universe in being able to maintain a nominal policy rate as low as 2.00% and a real interest rate close to 0%?
 That Sweden has considerable monetary policy room for manoeuvre was confirmed by Governor Thedéen in several interviews already on Wednesday: there is no need to rush into the next hike. 
SEB’s official forecast is now for the policy rate to peak at just 2.25%
, which could be regarded as a neutral rate. One hike has thus been removed from our forecast. Meanwhile, markets are pricing in a terminal rate of around 2.60%. 
But the key message to households and businesses remains unchanged: 
we are not heading back to the previous rate peak of 4%
.
 And that comes from someone who helped draft the Riksbank’s press release when the policy rate was raised to 500% 😊.
At last, a decisive moment.
 Sweden's Andersson’s latest revelation that her “government” would consist of the Social Democrats, Centre Party and Greens (S+C+MP) – with no Left Party ministers (V) – raises the stakes, adding to the (S)tress. There is also a tactical game at play: identifying the scapegoat (=V) if the baton (and C) is passed to the Moderates (M) to form a government.

articles.title: AI är inte svart eller vitt – perspektiv på dramatisk vecka
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Finansmarknader med stora problem att dra slutsatser – reflektioner.
 Ett högst 
väntat
 maktskifte i USA-kongressens båda kamrar – men med ett 
oväntat
 tydligt politiskt utfall
 – gav upphov till dramatiska marknadsrörelser när alla försöker dra kort- och långsiktiga slutsatser om konsekvenserna för ekonomin, teknologin och geopolitiken. 
Den positiva börsreaktionen i onsdags förvånade undertecknad lika mycket som den kraftigt negativa reaktionen i torsdags.
 Att AI- och techsektorn bör möta tilltagande motvind i USA – och på andra håll – visste vi ju redan före mellanårsvalet. Att 
Trump och republikanerna de närmaste två åren
 nu behöver föra en inrikes-, utrikes-, säkerhets- och handelspolitik som ger väljarna och företagen lägre (energi)priser och räntor, och som gör verklighet av orden ”America First”, kan på sikt verka lugnande på marknaden. Men den som tror att Trump nu blir mer förutsägbar, t o m samarbetsvillig, riskerar att gå fel. 
Utnämningen av Miller till ny stabschef bekräftar detta.
Uppstuds med viss tvekan – slutsatser.
 USA-börserna rekylerade upp i fredags efter torsdagens stora fall. S&P 500 och Nasdaq stängde 0,3% respektive 1,1% högre. Därmed backade tekniktunga Nasdaq med 3,4% under veckan, vilket raderade ca en tredjedel av årets uppgång. Analytiker – och ekonomer – behöver nu kunna skilja mellan aktuella AI-värderingar och de transformerande teknologiernas långsiktiga effekter på tillväxt, inflation och produktivitet. Att USA:s ekonomi har goda tillväxtutsikter bekräftades i fredags av ett 
nytt styrkebesked från USA:s arbetsmarknad
. Marknaden sätter nu 76% sannolikhet för att Fed höjer räntan till 4,25% den 9 december. Oljan handlas tidig måndag till 
98
 dollar per fat (Brent); 
16
% lägre på en vecka. B
eskeden från Nvidia om dels 
utredningen kring läckta uppgifter
, dels 
Jensens otrohetsaffär
, bidrar till en viss nervositet kring bolaget. Börserna i Asien följer uppgången efter USA:s
 fredagsrekyl. Börsterminerna handlas lite avvaktande, men med en positiv underton. 
Inte svart eller vitt – AI:s potential extremt svår att överblicka.
 I dag finns en frestelse att betrakta AI-teknologin som antingen frälsare eller hot, som himmel eller helvete. Sanningen ligger någonstans däremellan. Frågan är bara var. 
Lästips:
Affärsvärlden-krönika – ”AI ritar om kartan för centralbankerna”
.
Putin vill ha fredssamtal – men vill han ha fred?
 I morgon hålls trilaterala samtal (Ukraina, Ryssland och USA) på tjänstemannanivå i Abu Dhabi. Mötet väntas pågå i två dagar och ska fokusera på bl a säkerhetsgarantier och steg för att deeskalera kriget. 
Kremls fortsatta aggressiva agerande visar dock få tecken på fredsvilja
. Men det faktum att maktbalansen i USA-kongressen har ändrats (visserligen först med verkan fr o m 3 januari 2027) kan tillföra nya taktiska inslag i fredsprocessen. Men det förtjänas att upprepas: 
Trumps oförutsägbarhet är skriven i sten
.
Premiärministerskifte?
 Israels president 
Herzog ger Netanyahu-utmanaren Gadi Eisenkot
 (ledare för det nystartade partiet Yashar) i uppdrag att under 28 dagar – med möjlighet till förlängning – försöka samla en koalition med majoritet i Knesset. Även dessa politiska förhandlingar sker i en ny USA-kontext. Läget i Mellanöstern är fortsatt allvarligt och risken för nya omfattande 
amerikanska anfall
 kvarstår efter USA-valet. 
Noterat
 – 
Qatar vill få fram ett avtal som ger FN kärnvapeninspektörer tillgång till Irans kärnanläggningar
.
Klimatet – i dag inleds COP31.
 Följ nyhetsrapporteringen och den senaste utvecklingen via 
denna länk
.
Sverige
Äntligen ett avgörande läge.
 Anderssons nya besked – att hennes ”regering” består av S+C+MP (= inga V-ministrar) – höjer insatserna under (S)tress. Det handlar också om ett taktiskt spel: att peka ut syndabocken (=V) om stafettpinnen (och även C) går vidare till M för att bilda regering 
–
 eller om det blir extraval. Känslan infinner sig att vi nu står inför ett efterlängtat avgörande i regeringsfrågan.
Är vi ensamma i universum?
 Morgondagens protokoll – från den 3 november då riksbanksdirektionen enhälligt beslutade att höja styrräntan till 2,00% – framstår redan som dammigt p g a den 
överraskande låga oktoberinflationen
. Men penningpolitiken är förstås framåtblickande. Det finns tecken – t ex prisplaner och anekdotisk information – på att pristrycket stiger framöver, men utan dramatik. Att andra centralbanker, t ex Fed, ECB och Norges Bank, har klart högre styrräntor och i vissa fall väntas höja igen gör frågan relevant: 
är vi ensamma i universum om att kunna ha en nominell styrränta på låga 2,00% och en realränta nära 0%?
 Att Sverige har stort penningpolitiskt manöverutrymme bekräftade Thedéen i olika intervjuer redan i onsdags: vi behöver inte rusa vidare mot nästa höjning. 
SEB:s officiella prognos är att räntan planar ut redan på 2,25%
, vilket kan ses som en normalränta. En höjning har därmed tagits bort. Marknaden prisar samtidigt in en ränta som planar ut på ca 2,60%. 
Men det viktiga budskapet till hushåll och företag är oförändrat: vi ska inte tillbaka till den tidigare räntetoppen på 4%
. Detta sagt av en person som var med och skrev Riksbankens pressmeddelande när styrräntan höjdes till 500%
😊
.

articles.title: Payrolls a signal of continued strong momentum
articles.heading: US Economy
articles.fulltext:
Payroll employment (NFP) growth exceeded all estimates in October and there were also some upward revisions to the previous months. Employment data is very volatile, but the latest numbers support a continued strong momentum in the economy. This is a signal to the Fed that there is a need for some additional tightening though fears about AI and falling stock markets are currently working in the other direction. 
Key points
Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165k (estimated 70k, previous 60k, revised from 29k)
Upward revisions of 84k over the past two months
Unemployment rate 4.1% (estimated unchanged at 4.2%)
Labour force participation rate 61.9% (estimated unchanged at 61.8%)
Hourly earnings 0.4%, 3.1% y/y (estimated 0.3%, 2.9% y/y, previous 0.3%, 3.2% y/y, revised from 0.1%, 3.0% y/y)
Support for a December rate hike but equity markets and CPI inflation next week will be key
Robust but volatile employment growth 
US employment growth once again surprised massively on the upside, and this time on the strong side. We always expected to see some rebound from the weak August data, which seems to have been affected by large swings in hiring during the summer within e.g. government and leisure and entertainment, but not to this extent. Employment growth in October at 159k was above all economists’ expectations. The revision picture changed again, as well, with +84k for the previous two months and 3 months in a row with upward revisions. 
Longer 6-month trend better aligned with the new normal
Given the high volatility it is better to look at the longer trend. The 6-month average at 82k is below the pre-pandemic average of 180k-200k which is healthy given the slowdown in the labour force growth due to halted immigration/increased deportations. We view the current 6-month pace as slightly above the new break-even level of around 50k 
but given that payrolls tend to exaggerate the final estimate in employment it may not be that far above.
A sign of strong economic momentum
Even if payrolls show a high monthly volatility the outcome for October support a still strong momentum in economic activity. Another sign of strength is that employment growth is not only reflecting increased demand for workers in non-cyclical sectors such as education, health care and government, which were the main drivers in the previous years. In October, there were solid increases within manufacturing (19k), transportation (25k) and professional business services (70k). Leisure and hospitality (-13k) showed the largest monthly declines in October, while sectors more exposed to AI such as information (-1k) and finance (7k) were not as weak as in previous months. 
Unemployment in line with a balanced labour market
Unemployment edged lower in October, from 4.2 to 4.1%, still in line with the Fed’s view of the longer-run non-inflationary rate. Unemployment is unchanged over the past 2 ½+ years but trended higher in 2025, causing the Fed to cut rates three times, before trending lower again in 2026. A recovery in the participation rate and the labour force contributed to the decline in unemployment in October. This comes after a clear downward trend for especially participation since the implementation of new harsh immigration policies by President Trump, which has only been partly reversed.
The labour market is still not a risk to inflation
As long as there are no clear downtrends for unemployment, we think the Fed will not be worried about overheating risks from the labour market. This conclusion is supported by still modest earnings growth. The increase in October (0.4%, 3.1% y/y) was above expectations and there were also some upward revisions to the previous month, but earnings growth is fully consistent with the inflation target, given productivity growth at or slightly above 2% y/y. 
October jobs data supports December hike but CPI (and equity markets?) more important
We would be cautious to draw conclusions for the labour market from single months given the high volatility and many revisions of this data. We think the same is true for the Fed. However, October labour market data should not change the plans for another – and we believe final – rate hike at the December meeting. Next week’s CPI data will be even more important after the strong employment data, but the Fed is probably also closely following developments in equity markets and the faltering confidence in the AI expansion. A continued stock market decline could make the Fed pause given the importance of positive wealth effects for consumer spending. However, we would need to see much steeper declines to stop a December rate hike.
Going forward, labour market indicators such as small business hiring plans and employment indices in surveys have stabilised and even improved since the weakness in 2025, though households remain concerned about the availability of jobs. Jobless claims continue to show very limited layoffs. This supports that the labour market will remain in balance within a continued low-hiring, low-firing environment.

articles.title: Focus on central banks’ communication and inflation
articles.heading: The Week Ahead
articles.fulltext:
US inflation data and several Fed speeches will be in focus, with markets looking for clues about another rate hike in December. In the euro area, inflation and GDP data will provide further guidance on the economic outlook and ECB policy expectations. In Sweden, the Riksbank minutes will be closely watched for signals about further rate hikes, while Norwegian inflation data will be important for Norges Bank's next steps.  
US:
Focus on inflation data – CPI and PPI – and how this may affect expectations for another rate hike from the Fed in December. Because of last year’s government shutdown, the BLS will not be able to publish y/y CPI data. There will also be several appearances and speeches from members of the Fed, who may highlight their views at the time of the October rate decision and developments thereafter, including a possible continued stock market unrest coupled to AI fears after US midterm elections. As usual, speeches from vice Chair, the New York Fed’s John Williams, and board member Christopher Waller will be of particular interest. 
Euro area: 
Final October inflation figures for major economies, along with revised Q3 GDP and labour market data for the euro area, will provide further insights into price pressures and economic activity. We will also keep an eye on several ECB speeches. Finally, key EU meetings will take place, with budget issues, policy priorities and the succession of ECB President Lagarde likely to be discussed.
Sweden:
The Riksbank minutes is the main event this week. Growth metrics and the final CPI are the most important macro data. On Tuesday, Ulf Kristersson will report on his attempts to form a government to the parliament Speaker.
Norway:
October CPI-ATE is the highlight. Core inflation held steady at 3.0% y/y in September, 0.1pp above Norges Bank’s estimate. We expect it to ease to 2.8% in October, still 0.1pp above the bank’s forecast. Q4 consumer confidence will offer an important gauge on household demand, with sentiment deeply depressed since 2022. The Q4 Oil Investment Survey will likely bring some upward revisions to investment estimates but should still indicate that the investment cycle has peaked, with investment growth set to decline 2027.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Sweden
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
The growth momentum is currently strong, and we raise our 2026 GDP forecast. Headwinds from higher energy prices and mortgage rates will weigh on growth and the forecast for 2027 has been revised lower. The labour market is starting to improve but indicators imply a modest recovery in the near-term. Dovish signals from the Riksbank and lower-than-expected inflation imply postponed and more modest policy tightening. We predict a second rate hike in March and that the policy rate thereafter remains unchanged at 2.25 per cent until the end of 2028.  
According to the less-than reliable flash estimate, GDP in Q3 was largely in line with our forecast. However, we now predict the final Q3 GDP figure to be revised slightly higher and have raised our 2026 GDP forecast to 3.0 percent from 2.7 percent. The forecast for 2027 has, however, been lowered to 2.5 per cent (from 2.9 per cent) due to slower household consumption growth. 
After being very strong during the spring and summer, household consumption will face headwinds during the winter from high energy prices and rising mortgage rates. Consumption will slow to 2.3 per cent in 2027 from 3.0 per cent in 2026. In addition, several subsidies are being ended (lower fuel tax, public transportation), adding to the headwind. 
Industrial indicators have continued to improve and look very strong in an international comparison. Optimism is broad-based, although some traditional industries are more subdued. Exports and fixed investment will be the main drivers of growth in 2027.
Accelerating growth is starting to affect the labour market positively but the recovery is still modest, and indicators suggest that it will continue to be so over the next 3-6 months. Unemployment is starting to decline but continues to be high and indicators for capacity utilisation have improved only marginally from low levels. Labour unions’ demands ahead of the 2027 wage negotiations are somewhat lower than in 2025. Our and the Riksbank’s forecast that total wages will rise by slightly above 3 per cent in 2027 and 2028 seems to be largely on track. 
Core inflation has remained below the target even when excluding the lowered VAT on food and subsidies for public transport. A slightly weaker SEK and indirect effects from energy will temporary push CPIF ex energy above the target in 2027. Rising energy prices, partly because of a normalisation of fuel taxes, will temporarily push headline inflation to around 3 percent in the first half of 2027. In 2028, both measures are expected to fall towards target. 
The Riksbank is expected to raise the policy to 2.25 per cent in March and remain at this level until the end of 2028. Stronger growth implies that there are upside risks to our rate forecast.
Fiscal policy will gradually become more contractionary. The political deadlock makes the outlook highly uncertain and risks leading to less expansionary policy. 
On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts.

articles.title: The Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for an End to the Iran War
articles.heading: Conflict Update
articles.fulltext:
The midterms may have given the Trump administration its strongest signal yet that its war of choice in Iran has become deeply unpopular. But while Trump’s desire for an exit is a necessary condition for an end to the Iran War, it is not sufficient. For the conflict to end, both sides must prefer settlement to continuation. There must also be a significant zone of overlap between the two sides’ minimum terms as well as a sequencing formula that gets both sides past the commitment problem that made the Islamabad MoU so inherently fragile. The midterms have arguably strengthened Trump’s motive to end the war, but absent momentum on a zone of overlap and the right sequencing, ending the conflict could still prove challenging. Therefore, the main hurdles to a settlement at this point is not US voter preferences, but what level of strategic failure the Trump administration is willing to acknowledge, and the Trump administration’s capacity to manage a process that results in a diplomatic settlement.
The Iranian regime’s incentives to concede on key US-Israel demands have likely weakened
In Tehran, the midterm result will likely be interpreted as a sign that its war strategy has worked, implying that it will maintain, or even harden, its stance.
In October, Iran attacked more ships in or around Hormuz than in any month since February, with the aim of countering rising oil shipments with higher global prices. Higher energy prices have been a central instrument for deepening Trump’s political troubles and deterring another round of US strikes. The first days of this month have seen 
continued
 attacks on shipping in the area. 
Markets now price in a lower probability of US strikes post-midterm which raises the pressure on Iran as long as the US is not forthcoming with a diplomatic solution. This is because high oil prices and pressure on the global economy are a key instrument in the Iranian war strategy. An end to the war without its demands met is not an attractive scenario for the Iranian regime. 
Before the war, US demands centered on a full dismantlement of Iran’s nuclear program, significant restrictions on its ballistic missile program, and ceasing support for its affiliated militias in the region (Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias etc.). With the way the war has progressed, the Iranian regime is unlikely to concede to the level sought by the US, given the still limited set of concessions it can now feasibly get from the US. Therefore, the best the US can hope for in a near-term deal is that the volume of traffic through Strait of Hormuz returns to something akin to normal, albeit with greater Iranian control and rents generated from it. It may also be able to extract some marginal concessions on Iran’s nuclear program, and in October Vice President JD Vance stated that he wanted Iran to do something “
meaningful
” on its enrichment capacity. Yet since the Supreme Leader has listed as 
red lines
 the right to enrich uranium and the possession of enriched uranium stocks, progress in this area will be difficult for now. 
Trump arguably wants a diplomatic victory, but his personal reluctance to appear weak, in addition to US strategic interests, may prevent a US policy pivot that could be perceived as caving in to Iranian demands. This could be exacerbated if Tehran reads Trump’s electoral setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. Meanwhile, a 
letter
 from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei noted that anyone who expects that by “giving concessions to the United States, they can dissuade it from its hostility towards the Iranian nation, they are deeply mistaken.” Senior officials have also 
maintained
 that Iran’s strategy does not hinge on US elections. 
Economic pressure on Iran is substantial, but so is its ability to absorb it. The World Bank projects a 
7.7% GDP
 contraction for Iran in 2026, and the IMF projects a contraction of 
7.6%.
 The current regime leadership may judge that the prospect of scoring a strategic victory is worth economic costs to be borne over generations. 
Iran’s demands vary in feasibility
Lifting the blockade will likely be part of an arrangement, partly because it may be costly for the US armed forces to maintain anyway and is instrumental in getting Iran to cease disrupting shipping in the region. Restoring oil waivers, even if only temporarily, would also be a key to reducing Iranian incentives for regional disruption. The release of frozen assets, which has been part of negotiations for a long time, is relatively modest in size (in June, the discussion was about a 
release
 of USD 24bn in two installments) making it among the least problematic factors (even if it carries significant symbolic weight). And even lifting the 2026 sanctions, i.e. those imposed by the US after July this year, should be feasible. US force reductions in the region have already occurred, and a number of analysts have argued that the pre-war deployment is 
untenable
. 
Many of the additional demands are much more difficult for the US to acquiesce to. Iranian demands for US reparations for the war, and the costs it has imposed on Iran, are likely non-starters. Others may be more feasible, but still quite challenging. These includes Iran’s requirement that any ceasefire extends to “all fronts”, notably Lebanon. Yet a ceasefire on the Lebanon front is something Israel has more control over than the US. And as long as Hezbollah wields significant military power in the region, Israel is unlikely to go along with this. It is also unclear whether this extends to the separate, ongoing fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, putting significant pressure on Saudi Arabia, are currently looking to push through Taiz to capture Aden in the south of Yemen. The group has reportedly demanded USD 51bn to halt hostilities and requires Saudi Arabia to “officially recognize the militants as the rulers of Yemen,” according to the 
WSJ
. A ceasefire on all fronts could thus be hard to enforce for either side. 
Another difficult point is the future of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants the US to recognize the new shipping route in the 
Strait of Hormuz
 designated by Iran and Oman as the primary one. This represents a chokepoint risk for the Gulf states and the international shipping system more broadly, not just for the US. Some Iran analysts have warned of an attempt to turn the strait into an “
Iranian lake
”. Control of the chokepoint opens up the possibility for significant rents for Iran, which could translate into greater economic empowerment and future power projection in the region. At the moment, both US and Israeli national security planners are likely to see this as a zero-sum game, with Iran’s strategic gain being their loss. 
Poor sequencing and a lack of credible commitment remain binding constraints
Even where the principles of what each side should offer could be agreed, the sequencing and implementation of any arrangement are now bogged down by mistrust and suspicion. Each side’s preferred sequence is essentially for the other side to move first. Iran, as per statements by Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council 
Mohsen Rezaei
, requires good faith before Iran engages, including the frozen funds returned; the port blockade, reimposed on July 14th, lifted; nuclear talks last. Vance has said the sides “need to trade actions for actions.” 
The collapse of the MoU, along with the manner in which the US attacked Iran in February this year as well as in June last year, has made a new arrangement harder to reach. Iran remains hesitant to make stringent commitments without guarantees that US concessions—such as the lifting of oil export sanctions—will be permanent. 
Trump’s status as a lame duck limits his ability to negotiate from a position of strength. Iran may especially discount commitments from a lame-duck president, and much of the power of sanctions sits with Congress, which will be Democrat-controlled from January 3rd 2027. Given the expected investigations into the Trump administration, Congress could prove a troublesome partner for the president in ending the conflict in the Middle East. 
What could an arrangement look like? (And how easily it could fall apart)
A constructive trajectory would be for the parties to agree to a period where at least the following would occur: the release of a first instalment of frozen assets via Qatar and the lifting of the blockade, matched by an end to Iranian attacks on shipping and thus a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. This could be done over a relatively short period, and Qatar has already shortened Iran’s proposed timeline for reopening the Strait of Hormuz from seven days to two. The harder part is what the US would demand to allow sanctions waivers, and whether some of the post-July sanctions would be waived. Yet the US can realistically expect little here at this point.
A constructive process could include return of inspectors and elements of the JCPOA deal, but given the hardline nature of the new regime this seems a low-probability outcome. A ceasefire on all fronts also looks deeply challenging. Israel will likely oppose an arrangement that strengthens Iran, and thus the Lebanon front could remain more or less active. The Houthis have their own agenda in Yemen and arguably see a chance to strengthen their own lot, largely independent of Iranian near-term needs. This means both the US and Iran may struggle to secure compliance with ceasefires from two powerful regional actors. Domestic Iranian politics remain opaque, and an approaching end to the conflict could see the shifting political currents and infighting that complicate a durable diplomatic deal. And as noted above, Congress could directly or indirectly make the process more difficult if its coming political battles with the Trump administration make US-Iranian diplomacy harder. 
Each side needs a story it can sell at home
The Iranian regime needs a story of the war that cements its legacy and allows it to rewrite the national saga in which the regime is a savior rather than an oppressor. The concessions it can extract from the US and the region need to be weighed not just against the ongoing economic crisis, the tens of thousands who were killed in domestic repression only this year, but also against the decades of economic mismanagement, corruption, and oppression. Anything less risks regime instability, leaving distorted incentives in place where Iran’s ruling hardliners prefer the current situation of collective misery and insecurity to one where their long-term personal fortunes are more at risk.
Trump, meanwhile, needs an endgame in which he can still maintain the narrative of disrupting Iran’s nuclear ambitions, as well as one of regional progress with a smaller US economic footprint. Yet, depending on how the remainder of his presidency plays out, simply exiting to avoid of giving Congress yet another proverbial stick to beat him with may be enough to warrant pushing for an arrangement far below the administration’s initial ask. 
At this point, even without another round of escalation, the road to durable peace post-midterm looks precarious. Interim arrangements appear more likely than comprehensive deals. That said, a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz may not require the full set of demands on both sides to be met, and a more likely non-escalatory scenario is one where transit converges toward pre-war levels as Iran extracts some rents from the Strait without even if only a limited set of its demand, such as an end to the blockade and a release of frozen assets, have been met. Such an outcome would leave significant tension in place, reminding both sides that the alternative could be much worse, and would largely amount to mutual acceptance that both sides benefit from ending the war without a durable peace. 
Escalation threats remain
For now, the markets pricing in lower escalation appears somewhat premature. A president weakened in the midterms may seek “
redemption on the battlefield
,” even if much of the Trump administration’s electoral woes appear to stem from downstream of the Iran War. Before the vote, reports 
emerged
 that the US military has plans in place for resuming strikes with Iran after the midterms and allies in the Gulf region have been told to prepare for that eventuality. If Iran reads the midterms as leverage and holds out for more, a Trump who wants out but can’t get a deal he can sell may be pushed toward a short, sharp strike as a way out. And while the US in this scenario appears to plan for a short, intense conflict, Iran’s counterstrategy may be to absorb the strikes while maintaining military pressure on the region, risking a much wider, and more dangerous phase of the conflict. 
Source:
 "Iran War Chartpack Week 36: Calm Before The Storm?"
, SEB Conflict Update, November 4th 2026

articles.title: Muted manufacturing growth in Q3
articles.heading: Norwegian manufacturing production
articles.fulltext:
Manufacturing production was flat in September and rose just 0.1% in Q3. The composition of output growth was mixed; petroleum-related manufacturing dragged the overall figures down while traditional manufacturing basket limited the decline. The figures offer useful input ahead of the Q3 mainland GDP growth release on November 26. A sharp fall in electricity production will weigh on mainland growth, while manufacturing & mining will offer little contribution. Improving manufacturing sentiment, led by intermediate goods producers, points to broadly stable production growth ahead. 
Manufacturing Production: 
Manufacturing production was unchanged in September, leaving production up a modest 0.1% q/q in Q3. Annual growth picked up to 1.3%, from previously 0.4% in August (revised up from 0.2% y/y). Traditional-related manufacturing (0.4% m/m) offered some support to the monthly figures while petroleum-related production (-1.8% m/m) was a large drag. 
Details show that food, beverage and tobacco (1.7% m/m) rebounded strongly while wood and wood products (-4.6% m/m), rubber, plastic and mineral production (-4.1% m/m), basic metals (-5.1% m/m) and ships, boats and platforms (-3.9% m/m) all weighed on the monthly figures. 
Q3 figures suggest a neutral contribution to mainland GDP growth from manufacturing & mining, as output was broadly unchanged. Meanwhile, electricity production will likely be a drag on growth in Q3, with quarterly growth of -2.9%. 
Separately, construction data reports a 0.3% q/q increase in production in Q3. The 3m/3m rate has struggled to rise above zero since the first half of 2025 and should be welcome news for the depressed sector. Looking at the details, t
he largest categories specialized construction activities (0.7% q/q) and construction of buildings (0.3% q/q) lifted the quarterly figures, accounting for ~ 90% of the construction production index. Within construction of buildings, a large positive contribution came from development of building projects (1.2% q/q) while construction of residential and non-residential buildings (0.0% q/q) was flat in Q3.
 Civil engineering declined significantly (-2.1% q/q) but has a minor weight in these accounts. 
Industrial Production: 
Industrial production rose 1.0% m/m in September, but weakness earlier in the quarter left output down 1.8% q/q in Q3. Lower oil extraction weighed on the quarterly figures, partly offset by higher gas extraction. Support activities to oil production was broadly stable in Q3. Overall, the figures point to a negative contribution from industrial production to total GDP growth in Q3.

articles.title: AI panic on Wall Street
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
There were dramatic stock market falls in the US yesterday, with the S&P 500 falling 4.4% and the Nasdaq plummeting 5.5% in the worst daily decline since "Liberation Day" last year. After the initial relief rally on Wednesday that was driven by hopes that the Democrats' election victory will lead to a quick end to the Iran war, the market yesterday instead went "all in" on concerns that the AI rollout will now be halted as there is a compact resistance among Democrats to building more data centers. Although all AI companies were affected, it was toughest for the chipmakers. Nvidia ended at -9%, Broadcom at -10% and AMD fell more than 17%. AI companies outside the stock market are also feeling the brunt of the turmoil and for Anthropic, which is planning to start its IPO, the timing could hardly have been worse. The Musk companies also continued to suffer from the political hangover and SpaceX fell 9% while Tesla plummeted by almost 11%. 
In Asia, the sharp stock market falls continue
 this morning with the Nikkei at -6% and the Kospi at -5%. Ahead of the opening here at home, stock market futures still point to a calmer end to the week and it is only a percent down in Europe and actually a little up in the US. Given the drama on the stock exchanges, it has still been surprisingly calm in the currency markets, even though the dollar has strengthened a against other currencies in a classic risk-off move.
Among other news
 , we note that over half a million French people participated in yesterday's general strike for better study conditions, higher wages and a better welfare. Hmm, it will probably be difficult to get those demands to go together with the fiscal situation...
Focus on Payrolls and Sölvesborg. 
 Although the stock market panic and the aftermath of the election will continue to be in focus today, we will also get jobs numbers from the US, as usual on the first Friday of a new month. Last month was weak and although the signals from the labor market are mixed, the market expects a figure around 50k in October and a stable unemployment rate of 4.2%. Such an outcome would also be well in line with the Fed's view of the situation. For Sweden, all eyes are now on the town of Sölvesborg, where Sd party leader Jimmie Åkesson will hold a press conference at lunchtime on the government issue.
Nordic key stories
Yesterday Norges Bank 
kept the policy rate unchanged at 4.50%, as widely expected. The Committee concludes that economic developments and inflation prospects appear to be broadly as envisaged. Given limited new data released since September, it is unsurprising that the Committee wants to await more input before reassessing its policy stance. The guidance from September was thus reiterated: “…the outlook implies that it will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time. The Committee is prepared to raise the policy rate further if warranted by the inflation outlook”. We still believe the policy rate has peaked, although risks remain skewed to the upside.
Swedish house prices in October. 
 This morning, new data from Mäklarstatistik showed prices for tenant-owned apartments rose by 1.9% (5.8% y/y), while detached houses fell by 0.6% (4.2% y/y).
Reading today. 
 Over the past week, we have published updated macro forecasts for different countries under the heading Nordic Outlook Update. Last out is Sweden, which will be published on SEB's research page during the day.
Have a great Friday.

articles.title: AI-panik på Wall Street
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Det var dramatiska börsfall i USA igår. S&P 500 föll 4,4% och Nasdaq rasade hela 5,5% i den värsta dagliga nedgången sedan ”Liberation Day” i april 2025 då Trump lanserade sina planer på nya tullar. Efter det initiala lättnadsrallyt i onsdags som drevs av förhoppningar att demokraternas valseger ska leda till ett snabbt slut på Irankriget gick marknaden igår istället ”all in” på oron för att AI-utbyggnaden nu ska stoppas då det finns ett kompakt motstånd hos demokraterna mot att bygga fler datacenter. Även om alla AI-bolag drabbades så var det tuffast för chiptillverkarna. Nvidia slutade på -9%, Broadcom på -10% och AMD föll mer än 17%. Även AI-bolag utanför börsen lär känna av oron och för Anthropic som ligger i startgroparna för sin IPO kan tajmingen knappast ha varit värre. Musk-bolagen fortsatte också att må dåligt av politisk baksmälla och SpaceX föll 9% medan Tesla rasade med nästan 11%. Man undrar när övriga aktieägare i dessa bolag ska börja se sin yviga vd som en belastning snarare än en tillgång?
I Asien fortsätter de kraftiga börsfallen
 nu på morgonen med Nikkei på -6% och Kospi på -5%. Inför öppningen här hemma pekar börsterminerna ändå mot en lugnare avslutning på veckan och det är bara någon procent ned i Europa och faktiskt lite upp i USA. Givet dramatiken på börserna så har det ändå varit förvånansvärt lugnt på valutamarknaderna även om dollarn har stärkts lite mot övriga valutor enligt ett klassiskt risk-off-mönster.
Hur orolig ska man vara för AI-traden? 
Även om börsrörelserna är dramatiska tycker i alla fall undertecknad att det finns flera skäl till att se lite positivt på läget om man höjer blicken. 
1)
 Det finns inte mycket som tyder på att redan beslutade datacenterprojekt kommer att stoppas och det gör att AI-utbyggnaden kommer fortsätta enligt plan nästa år. 
2)
 Det ger också AI-bolagen tid att ställa om och generellt ska man inte underskatta näringslivets förmåga att anpassa sig till nya förutsättningar. Det finns många delstater i USA som kommer vilja ha de investeringar och jobb som utbyggnaden ger och datacenter kan också byggas utanför USA. 
3)
 Man kan också fundera kring om det inte faktiskt kan vara en välbehövlig avkylning av en sektor där oron så sent som förra veckan handlade om att den är alldeles för överhettad. En lugnare utbyggnadstakt skulle också ge hyperscalers som Alphabet, Microsoft och Meta bättre marginaler och kassaflöden. 
4)
 På den positiva sidan finns också att en lugnare utbyggnadstakt både minskar inflationsriskerna och därmed behovet av räntehöjningar och minskar konkurrensen om investeringskapital som varit en viktig drivkraft bakom stigande långräntor de senaste månaderna.
Bland övriga nyheter
 noterar vi att över en halv miljon fransmän deltog i gårdagens generalstrejk för bättre studievillkor, högre löner och en bättre välfärd. Hmm, kan nog bli svårt att få de kraven att gå ihop med den statsfinansiella kalkylen…
Fokus på Payrolls och Sölvesborg. 
Även om börspaniken och efterdyningarna av valet kommer fortsätta att stå i centrum idag får vi, som vanligt den första fredagen i en ny månad, också jobbsiffror från USA. Förra månaden var svag och även om signalerna från arbetsmarknaden är blandade så räknar marknaden med en siffra runt 50k i oktober och stabil arbetslöshet på 4,2%. Ett sådant utfall skulle också ligga väl i linje med Feds syn på läget. För svensk del riktas blickarna idag mot Sölvesborg där Jimmie Åkesson vid lunchtid ska hålla en presskonferens om regeringsfrågan. Spännande! 
Sverige
Högre bostadsrättspriser i oktober. 
Nu på morgonen kom nya siffror från Mäklarstatistik. I riket steg priserna på bostadsrätter med 1,9% (5,8% å/å) medan villor backade med 0,6% (4,2% å/å).
Lästips idag. 
Den senaste veckan har vi publicerat uppdaterade makroprognoser för olika länder under rubriken Nordic Outlook Update. Sist ut är Sverige, som kommer publiceras på SEB:s research-sida under dagen.
Ha en bra fredag.

articles.title: United on the hike, divided on the path
articles.heading: Bank of England
articles.fulltext:
A unanimous hike, more hawkish than expected
The vote was 0–9: all nine members voted for a hike, with Catherine Mann preferring 50bp to 4.25%. The two most dovish members, Taylor and Dhingra, also backed a hike, which made the decision more hawkish than we expected.
Inflation forecast revised up, stronger growth adds to the case
There is still limited evidence of second-round effects, but upside inflation risks have increased. In the run-up to the meeting, Brent crude oil and UK gas futures averaged 38% and 81% higher than at the time of the July Report, and above the July adverse scenario. According to the MPC, firms have so far absorbed the price increases through lower profit margins, but at least parts of these cost pressures are likely to feed through to consumer prices eventually. The MPC judges that “the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate”.
The inflation forecast was revised up, and the BoE now sees inflation peaking at 4.9% in Q2 2027 before returning to target in Q3 2028. The central projection also assumes larger second-round effects than in July, although not at severe levels, and these are partly offset by the relief measures in the Budget. Stronger growth and activity data add to the case for hiking. Growth was revised up for 2026, although the BoE still judges that there is a margin of slack in the economy. It expects growth to slow in 2027 as real incomes are squeezed, and unemployment to rise modestly.
One-and-done or the start of a cycle?
The MPC put more emphasis on a data-dependent approach: “Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path”. The Committee will assess how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the wider economy, for example by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour and slack.
MPC members still judge that the policy rate is restrictive and the individual statements show a committee that leans towards at least one more hike, but not a full cycle. The most hawkish member, Mann, voted for 50bp on risk-management and credibility grounds, pointing to non-linear effects now that inflation has crossed key thresholds. At the other end, the most dovish member, Taylor, stated explicitly that this is not the start of a hiking cycle and that the next move could be “up, down, or sideways”, even if we could rule out at least one of the alternatives. 
Pushback against market pricing
The BoE pushes back on the market path further out, as they have done in previous 
research
. On market pricing, Bailey said that some of the upward slope in the curve is explained by risk premia rather than expected rates. This stems from the usage of OIS contracts for hedging together with the current market view of asymmetric inflation, and consequently interest rate risks. Calculating the implied rate from Polymarket’s contract may give a less distorted measure. Nevertheless, economists remain on the dovish side in this call, and so do we.
Neutral to hawkish market reaction
Gilt yields rose by 6bp in the short end and 4bp at the 10-year point. The implied rate for the December meeting signals a ~50% probability of a hike. For the February meeting the probability is higher, with an implied rate of about 4.30%. The unanimous vote and the hawkish individual statements outweighed the MPR’s pushback against market pricing, and the terminal market-implied rate rose by roughly 6bp. The GBP initially strengthened by about 0.3% against the euro and the dollar but has since fallen back to roughly pre-meeting levels.
Our call
We are revising our call and adding another hike in February, as the BoE tends to move at meetings where it can back the decision with a new Monetary Policy Report and updated forecasts. However, given the already restrictive policy stance, weaker projected growth in 2027 and coming base effects that will pull down headline inflation, we see no immediate reason to add further hikes than that. With inflation being persistently higher for longer, we also postpone the first cut into 2028. In our base case, the front end of the gilt curve would start to shift down some time after the February hike. This would likely spill over to the longer end as well, which is seen declining on the back of lower rate expectations and a better outlook for government finances. However, like the BoE, we remain responsive if the data move against our call.
